blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: A multiplayer world model must predict how the independent actions of several players change a shared environment, including changes outside a player's current field of view. A point-of-view (POV) video captures such changes only after they enter its field of view, whereas panoramic video records the surroundings in every viewing direction and has served as an intermediate representation of the world state in recent world models. Learning this task therefore requires synchronized POV and panoramic videos of interacting players together with their actions, yet no existing dataset provides this combination in Minecraft, an established testbed in which players act independently in a shared, modifiable 3D world. We present PAWA, a dataset and framework for action-conditioned panoramic multiplayer world modeling. The dataset pairs each player's POV video with world-stabilized panoramic video and aligned actions. Its distributed pipeline decouples CPU gameplay capture from GPU rendering, scales beyond 64 simultaneous players, and re-renders each recorded session under new observation configurations without replaying the gameplay. On this dataset, we develop a dual-tower model that jointly predicts POV and panoramic video and couples the two streams through cross-attention that aligns tokens observing the same direction in a shared world frame. We further introduce a quadratic-phase player encoding that provides many more player codes than existing rotary codes at the same embedding dimension. Experiments show that PAWA outperforms state-of-the-art multiplayer world models in POV prediction quality while also producing high-fidelity panoramic predictions. The dataset and collection pipeline are open source to support further research on multiplayer world models.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
In a multiplayer world, several players act independently on a shared environment, and each
action can change what every other player sees. A world model for such a world must predict how
these combined actions unfold in each player’s observations. Many of the consequences arise
outside a player’s field of view. A teammate places a block behind the player, or an opponent
approaches from the side, and the change becomes visible only once the camera turns toward it.
A point-of-view (POV) video therefore records the shared world only in part. Panoramic video
records the surroundings in every direction at once, and recent world models have adopted it as
a representation of the surrounding scene and as spatial
memory ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Pairing each player’s POV video
with a panorama exposes the surroundings of every player to the model, including the regions
that no local camera currently observes.

Minecraft offers a natural setting, since players act independently in a
shared 3D world that every action can modify. It is an established testbed for
action-conditioned video world
models ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; He et al., 2025 ) , and
recent multiplayer models synchronize the POV videos of several interacting
players ( Savva et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2026a ) . These multiplayer models
learn from perspective observations alone. Other multi-agent world models broaden visual
coverage by stitching directional views into panoramas ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) or by
projecting panoramic recordings into perspective training views ( Sun et al., 2026a ) , yet
their generated streams remain perspective videos. Predicting full-sphere panoramic
video jointly with each player’s POV under the actions of interacting players remains
unexplored.

blocks.en:
Modeling POV and panoramic video together for many players raises three challenges. (i) Paired multiplayer data. Existing multiplayer data are recorded by screen
capture from live game clients, which yields only the displayed perspective view. Every player
also requires its own graphics client, and the recording cost therefore grows with the
population. No dataset pairs POV and panoramic video with the actions of interacting players. (ii) Correspondence across projections. The same scene direction occupies
different image coordinates in a rectilinear POV frame and an equirectangular panorama. Because
the POV camera turns with the player’s head while the panorama stays fixed to the world, this
correspondence changes at every frame. (iii) Player identity at scale. A model that shares parameters across players
must keep each observation stream bound to its own actions. Existing rotary player codes admit
only m + 1 m+1 equidistant identities in m m phase planes ( Liu et al., 2026a ) , and the
identity pool therefore grows only linearly with the embedding dimension.

blocks.en:
In this paper, we present PAWA ( P anoramic A ction-conditioned W orld modeling for multiple A gents), a dataset and framework for action-conditioned panoramic
multiplayer world modeling in Minecraft. (i) Scalable, programmable collection. PAWA records gameplay on CPUs
without graphics clients, simulating sessions with more than 64 simultaneous players, and renders
the saved replays offline on GPUs. Each replay yields a player’s POV video, a world-stabilized
equirectangular panorama and aligned actions, and can be rendered again with relative depth or
along custom camera trajectories without repeating gameplay. These observations serve
multiplayer world modeling well beyond panoramic prediction. Coding agents compose interaction
scripts from natural-language descriptions, and behavioral checks together with vision-language
review retain the scripts whose intended interactions occur (Figure 2 ). (ii) Dual towers with ray-aligned cross-attention. A POV tower and a panorama tower jointly
predict the two videos and are repeatedly coupled through bidirectional ray-aligned
cross-attention. Each token carries its viewing ray in a shared world frame as a rotary phase, and tokens
that observe the same direction thus have zero relative phase regardless of their image coordinates
(Figure 3 ). The panorama thus serves as both a prediction target and a
source of context for the local view. In the resulting forecasts, a co-player seen in a player’s
POV appears in the matching direction of the same player’s panorama (Figure 1 ). (iii) Quadratic-phase player encoding. Building on classical quadratic-phase
codes ( Wootters and Fields, 1989 ) , PAWA assigns each player a rotary code from a pool of m 2 m^{2} identities in the same m m phase planes. The identity pool thus grows quadratically rather than linearly with the embedding
dimension.

blocks.en:
Our contributions are threefold. (i) We construct a multiplayer Minecraft dataset of
synchronized POV and world-stabilized panoramic videos with aligned actions, whose distributed
pipeline scales beyond 64 simultaneous players and re-renders replays with relative depth or
custom camera trajectories. Both are open source on Hugging Face and GitHub . (ii) We propose a dual-tower world model that jointly predicts POV and panoramic video,
whose ray-aligned cross-attention encodes world-frame viewing rays as rotary phases and thereby
assigns identical phases to matching viewing directions in the two projections. (iii) We introduce a quadratic-phase player encoding that enlarges the identity pool from m + 1 m+1 to m 2 m^{2} codes at a fixed embedding dimension, with closed-form correlations between any two
codes.

blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Interactive video world models. World models predict the consequences of actions for
control ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2025 ) . Video world models learn this prediction
through autoregressive tokens ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , latent actions ( Bruce et al., 2024 ) ,
adapted video diffusion ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , and diffusion game
engines ( Alonso et al., 2024 ; Valevski et al., 2025 ; Kanervisto et al., 2025 ) , and now generate
gameplay, explorable scenes, and navigation views under user
control ( Che et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Mao et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026b ; Xiong et al., 2026 ; Bar et al., 2025 ) . Minecraft is a central testbed for
action-conditioned simulation ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; He et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) and for learned
agents ( Guss et al., 2019 ; Fan et al., 2022 ; Baker et al., 2022 ; Lifshitz et al., 2023 ) . Language models
write executable skills ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024a ) and vision-language models
judge task success ( Du et al., 2023 ) , and PAWA uses both to generate and
validate multiplayer interactions.

blocks.en:
Multiplayer world models. Multiplayer models render every player’s observation under
the combined actions of all players. Solaris, Gamma-World, and MIRA generate synchronized player
views in Minecraft and Rocket League ( Savva et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Hu et al., 2026a ) , and
further models coordinate views through shared world states, registers, or
memories ( Wu et al., 2026a ; Mo et al., 2026 ; Po et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Cai et al., 2026 ) .
Related work learns multi-agent generation from single-view footage ( Hu et al., 2026b ) ,
routes peer-view evidence ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , composes joint actions for
cooperation ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , and synthesizes surround views of a single
vehicle ( Wang et al., 2024c ; Wen et al., 2024 ; Russell et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) . ShareVerse and
Prisma-World widen coverage by stitching directional views or by cropping panoramic
recordings ( Zhu et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026a ) . Their generated streams remain
perspective videos, and their multiplayer data come from live game
clients ( Savva et al., 2026 ) . Like procedural generators that render programmable scenes
offline ( Greff et al., 2022 ; Deitke et al., 2022 ) , PAWA renders recorded gameplay into
aligned POV and panoramic videos, and it predicts both.

Panoramic video generation and world models. Panoramic video records the full
surroundings in every frame, and recent world models adopt it as the world representation
itself. Panoramas serve as proxies for explorable 3D
worlds ( HunyuanWorld Team, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Su et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) ,
for long-horizon and single-image
exploration ( Liu et al., 2026b ; Gui et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) , as latent states for
perspective rendering ( Tan et al., 2026 ) and driving ( Li et al., 2026a ) , and for
geometric consistency and spatial
memory ( Jiang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Jia et al., 2026 ) . These models build on
360-degree video diffusion ( Wang et al., 2024b ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Xia et al., 2025 ; Ji et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) , perspective-to-panorama
expansion ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026c ) , and joint perspective and
panoramic modeling ( Tang et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Tan et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2025 ) . Perspective models instead recall regions from visual
history ( Xiao et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025a ) or simulate out-of-sight
dynamics ( Duan et al., 2026 ) for a single observer. PAWA extends panoramic
prediction to a shared world, where each panorama reflects changes caused by co-players.

blocks.en: 3 Panoramic multiplayer dataset
blocks.zh: 3 全景多人数据集

blocks.en:
A panoramic multiplayer world model learns from both projections and the actions of every
player within one synchronized interaction. To this end, we construct a dataset that pairs each
player’s POV video with a world-stabilized panoramic video, aligned actions and camera
annotations. Existing multiplayer data such as the Solaris dataset are recorded from live
Minecraft clients ( Savva et al., 2026 ) , which limits each recording to the perspective view
displayed during play. Our pipeline instead records programmable interactions on CPUs and renders
the saved replays offline on GPUs, which yields POV and panoramic videos, relative depth and
custom camera trajectories from a single interaction without repeating the gameplay
(Figure 2 ).

blocks.en:
Scaling multiplayer data collection. SolarisEngine pairs each Mineflayer controller
with a live graphics client ( Savva et al., 2026 ) , and controller computation and rendering
therefore both grow with the player count and must keep pace with the running simulation.
PAWA removes rendering from gameplay. Its player runtime, built on the
open-source Azalea library, executes action scripts written in Rust and simulates interactions
among more than 64 simultaneous players while recording per-tick actions, positions, camera
orientations and player state. Without graphics clients, independent episodes run in parallel
across CPU hosts, and GPU workers render the saved replays on separate hosts, with views and
camera paths assigned to workers independently. Capture and rendering thus scale with separate
resources, and a large session is recorded once and rendered afterwards.

blocks.en:
Generating and validating interactions. Interaction scenarios are specified as
natural-language descriptions of player behaviors and expected outcomes. Coding agents
compose reusable interaction primitives into executable scripts, which may fail to produce their
intended interaction, and each scenario is therefore validated on both behavior and appearance.
Behavioral quality control (QC) detects inactivity, ineffective movement and abrupt control
changes in the recorded actions and states before rendering, and a vision-language model (VLM)
then reviews sampled videos against the specified outcomes. Both checks return feedback
for the coding agents to revise the scripts.

blocks.en:
Observing a shared world beyond the local view. Each player’s rectilinear POV video is
paired with an equirectangular panorama rendered from the same camera origin. The
panorama stays oriented to the world as the player’s head turns, which gives every frame a stable
directional reference and records changes that no local camera observes. All videos share the
server clock, and action annotations and camera poses bind each observation to
its player (Appendix 7 ).

blocks.en:

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We present PAWA, a dataset and framework for action-conditioned panoramic multiplayer
world modeling. Its pipeline turns sessions of more than 64 players into
synchronized POV and world-stabilized panoramic videos with aligned actions, and its model
jointly predicts both videos for every player through ray-aligned cross-attention and
quadratic-phase player codes. It outperforms state-of-the-art multiplayer world models in POV
prediction and produces high-fidelity panoramas.

我们介绍PAWA,一个数据集和具备行动条件的全景多人游戏机的框架
世界模特 它的管道将64个以上参与者的会话变成
同步 POV 和世界稳定全景视频,并配合动作,及其模式
通过射线相通的交叉注意,共同预测每个玩家的视频和
四相相玩家代码. 它超越了POV中最先进的多人世界模型
预测并产生高性能全景。

blocks.en:
Limitations and future work. Like all evaluated multiplayer world models, PAWA
loses co-player fidelity over long rollouts, and its POV and panoramic forecasts diverge gradually
since the cross-attention aligns directions without enforcing pixel agreement. Although the
pipeline records more than 64 players and the codebook provides 120 identities, the model does not
decouple the players, and its computational cost increases rapidly with the number of players,
which limits training and evaluation to sixteen players. Scaling to larger populations requires a
redesign in which each player runs on its own GPU and exchanges little information with the others.

Table 13 reports POV LPIPS in four forecast-frame bands, over the whole
frame and within co-player regions. Co-player regions are projected from the recorded player poses
with the box expansion and temporal union of Appendix 8.2 , HUD rows are excluded,
and a frame counts when the region covers at least 0.5% of the image. Over the 12-second
rollout, co-player LPIPS rises for every model, by 0.14 to 0.27 for Gamma-World, Solaris and
PAWA, and part of every increase reflects the recorded future diverging from the first
frame, since the LPIPS of the static copy rises by 0.11. In the last band, the co-player
regions of all Gamma-World variants, Solaris and MultiWorld are no closer to the reference than
this static copy, whereas both PAWA variants obtain a lower LPIPS. The same trend holds with
four players, where co-player LPIPS rises from 0.476 to 0.618 for PAWA (Distilled) and
from 0.547 to 0.719 for Gamma-World (Distilled). Loss of co-player fidelity over long rollouts is
therefore common to current multiplayer world models, and PAWA keeps the co-player
regions closest to the reference in every band.
